title: SYSK Selects: How Marijuana Works
summary: Saturday Selects rerun of the SYSK episode "How Marijuana Works." Chuck introduces it as a classic from the archives. The hosts give an overview of cannabis history from ancient China and Egypt through its US history: hemp farming in early America, the Mexican Revolution-era immigration and moral panic, Reefer Madness, the 1937 Marijuana Tax Act, Harry Anslinger, mandatory minimums in the 1950s and 1980s, and the Schaefer Commission under Nixon. They cover cannabis strains (indica vs. sativa), the plant's biology (sinsemilla, trichomes, THC), how THC affects the brain through the endocannabinoid system, the body and liver metabolism, addiction and withdrawal, drug testing, medical uses, legalization in Washington and Colorado, potency trends, smoking methods, and lung health. Listener mail from Andrew in Australia about firefighting closes the episode.
topics: marijuana history in the United States

segments.title: Introduction and Saturday Selects framing
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the classic episode as a Saturday Select. Josh and Chuck banter about the episode's approach and terminology for cannabis.

segments.title: Ancient history and cannabis species
segments.summary: The hosts cover cannabis use in ancient China, the Egyptian mummy with THC, the Arabian Nights reference, and the debate over origins. They discuss indica versus sativa and the effects and growth habits commonly attributed to each.

segments.title: Hemp in early America and the rise of prohibition
segments.summary: Hemp was widely grown in America and Virginia required farmers to grow it in the 1600s. Use declined in the early 1900s. The hosts discuss how Mexican immigration after 1910 and racially charged reporting fueled a moral panic, and why marijuana became a derogatory term.

segments.title: Reefer Madness, the 1937 Marijuana Tax Act, and Harry Anslinger
segments.summary: Reefer Madness is discussed as propaganda. The Marijuana Tax Act of 1937 effectively criminalized the drug through a tax, and Harry Anslinger of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics led the crusade. La Guardia's report found no link to violence or insanity.

segments.title: Mandatory minimums, the 1960s, Nixon, and the 1980s
segments.summary: Mandatory minimum sentences in the 1950s, relaxation in the 1960s with presidential reports, the gateway drug debate, the Schaefer Commission's decriminalization recommendation that Nixon rejected, and the Reagan-era Anti-Drug Abuse Act with plant-to-heroin weight comparisons. The hosts also discuss LSD sentencing by weight.

segments.title: Street prices and the dispensary market
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the price of marijuana by weight and quantity, how dealers and dispensaries operate similarly, and the mix of legal and formerly illegal growers now licensed. Edibles and cannabis strips are mentioned.

segments.title: The cannabis plant, sinsemilla, and trichomes
segments.summary: The palmate leaf, the flowering buds (sinsemilla), male versus female plants, pollen spread, hermaphroditic plants, the hundreds of chemicals including over a hundred cannabinoids, and THC stored in trichomes. Cultivators seek higher THC.

segments.title: How THC affects the body and brain
segments.summary: Using farmer Ted as an example, the hosts trace THC from smoking through the lungs and bloodstream to the brain. They explain how the endocannabinoid system is hijacked, affecting memory, coordination, fear, appetite, and dopamine release. Half-life and drug testing are covered as well.

segments.title: Ingestion, liver metabolism, and addiction
segments.summary: Eating cannabis produces a delayed, longer-lasting effect because the liver converts THC into another psychoactive compound. The hosts discuss Amsterdam edibles and then addiction and withdrawal symptoms, which they call psychological and habitual rather than classic addiction.

segments.title: Medical uses, Schedule I status, and legalization
segments.summary: Medical uses include appetite stimulation, glaucoma, epilepsy (CBD oil in Georgia), multiple sclerosis, cancer research, and arthritis. The drug remains a Schedule I substance. The hosts cover Colorado and Washington legalization, polling, and the Buzz Kill article on the economics of legal pot.

segments.title: Potency trends, smoking methods, and lung health
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the potency debate, the University of Mississippi Potency Monitoring Project, and how THC levels rose from 3.4 to 8.8 percent between 2000 and 2008. They cover joints, blunts, bongs, vaporizers, and teen use. A study found low to moderate use is less harmful to lungs than tobacco.

segments.title: Listener mail: Andrew the Australian smoke jumper
segments.summary: Andrew from Australia writes that the wildfire episode inspired him to volunteer with the Rural Fire Service and aim to become a smoke jumper.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts ask for listener life updates and direct listeners to social media and the website.
